title: Test a transformer
summary: Work out which winding is which, check for broken windings and leaks between windings and to the core with a meter, then power-test mains transformers through a dim-bulb tester. Microwave oven transformers get resistance checks only.

materials.item: Dim-bulb tester: an old-style filament bulb of 40–100 W in an insulated holder, wired in series with the transformer's mains lead
Fuse and holder rated for the transformer

steps.text: Read the label: input voltage, output voltage or voltages, VA or watts, and frequency. Note any wire colour list.
Look and smell. Burnt varnish, charred tape, melted plastic or bulging windings mean it has overheated.
With the meter on ohms, find which wires connect. Each winding is a pair of wires, or more if it has taps, that show continuity to each other and to no other wires.
On a step-down mains transformer, the mains (primary) winding has the higher resistance, usually tens to hundreds of ohms on small ones. The low-voltage winding reads much lower.
Check insulation on the highest ohms range: from each winding to every other winding, and from each winding to the metal core. Every reading should be OL.
steps.warn: Any reading between the mains winding and the low-voltage winding or the core makes the transformer unsafe to use.

steps.text: If the primary of a small transformer reads open, a thermal fuse buried under the outer tape may have blown. Replace it only with one of the same temperature and current rating.
steps.warn: Never bridge a thermal fuse with wire. It is what stops the transformer catching fire.

steps.text: Power test, mains transformers only: wire the primary through the fuse and the dim-bulb tester. Separate and tape every low-voltage wire. Then plug in.
steps.warn: Make every connection before you plug in. Keep your hands off while it is live, and unplug before touching anything.

steps.text: The bulb should glow briefly, then stay dim or dark. If it lights brightly and stays bright, a winding is shorted: unplug at once.
Measure the output on AC volts. With no load it usually reads 5–20% above the label, and small transformers can read even higher.
Microwave oven transformers (MOTs) get resistance tests only. The primary reads a fraction of an ohm; the high-voltage winding reads far higher, tens of ohms or more.
steps.warn: A MOT puts out about 2 kV at a current that kills. Don't power-test one with its high-voltage winding in place.

steps.text: Never feed power into the low-voltage side of a transformer.
steps.warn: A step-down transformer fed backwards steps the voltage up, putting mains voltage or more on the primary wires.

notes:
## How a dim-bulb tester works

    mains live ---[fuse]---[filament bulb]---+
                                             |  transformer primary
    mains neutral ---------------------------+

The bulb is in series with the transformer. A healthy transformer with nothing connected to its output draws little current, so the bulb barely glows. A shorted winding draws heavy current, the bulb lights up fully, and the bulb takes the voltage instead of your wiring.

It must be an old-style filament bulb. LED and compact fluorescent bulbs don't work in a dim-bulb tester. A 60 W bulb suits most small and medium transformers.

## Rough resistances

| Transformer | Primary (mains side) | Secondary |
|---|---|---|
| Small mains, under about 50 VA | tens to hundreds of ohms | a few ohms or less |
| Large mains, hundreds of VA | a few ohms or less | a fraction of an ohm |
| Microwave oven (MOT) | a fraction of an ohm | tens of ohms or more |

These are only a guide. What matters is that each winding reads something (not OL), and nothing reads between windings or to the core.

## Ferrite (switch-mode) transformers

The small transformers inside switch-mode power supplies run at tens of thousands of hertz. Never connect them to mains: they will short. Test them for continuity and insulation only.

## VA and watts

VA is volts × amps. A 12 V 50 VA transformer can supply about 4 A of AC. Rectified and smoothed into DC, it can supply noticeably less DC current, often around two-thirds of that.

## Common mistakes

- Using an LED bulb in the dim-bulb tester.
- Scrapping a transformer whose only fault is a thermal fuse.
- Leaving low-voltage wires touching during the power test.
- Power-testing a MOT.
